plain.li:
[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] Come sit and hear a traveller's tale,
for the road is long and the night is cold;
I walked from the hills to the edge of the sea
with a coat too thin and a heart too bold.

I traded my boots for a basket of bread,
I traded the bread for a song in the rain,
I traded the song for a place by a fire,
and I never once wished for my boots again.

So if ever you see a stranger come walking
with nothing to sell and a story to tell,
put a chair by the hearth and a bowl in their hands,
for they have walked the road, and the road has walked them as well.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences,!w:tribal] The river rose in the month of rain,
and it rose a hand each hour,
and the miller's daughter climbed the wheel
to stand above the flour.

She called the town to the high mill floor,
the young, the old, the lame,
and they sat on sacks while the water roared
and sang to keep from shame.

They sang the old songs and the new,
they sang them loud and long,
and when the morning came up grey
the river heard the song.

It bowed its back and it went away,
as rivers sometimes do,
and the miller's daughter climbed back down
and swept the floor anew.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] He rode out with the raiders at the turning of the year,
with a sword he had not paid for and a grin from ear to ear;
he came back in the springtime with the sword and not the grin,
and he sat down by his mother's door and would not come in.

They asked him what he'd taken, and he told them what he'd lost,
and he named the towns behind him, and he counted up the cost,
and the young ones who were listening went quietly to bed,
and not one of them rode out that year, or so the old ones said.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] There was a girl who kept the bees
up where the clover grows,
and every spring she spoke to them
the way a keeper knows.

She told them who was born that year,
she told them who had died,
she told them who had married whom
and who had stood beside.

And when she died, the bees were told,
by the youngest of her kin,
and the hives went quiet for a day,
and then they hummed again.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences,theirs] At {TOWN} there is a lamp that burns
all night beside the gate,
for anyone who's coming home
and finds that they are late.

It burned for soldiers, burned for wives,
for children lost and found,
for travellers with nowhere else,
for strays and for the drowned.

And if you ever pass that way
when all the town's asleep,
the lamp will burn for you as well;
that is a promise that we keep.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:spring] The thaw has come, the mud is deep,
the lambs are loud, and nobody sleeps;
the fields are wet, the roads are worse,
and I have written you this verse.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:autumn] The leaves come down, the stores go up,
the {ANIMALS} fatten, and so do we;
the evenings close like a folding hand
round a fire, and a pot, and company.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:winter] The snow is on the roof again,
and on the road, and on the hill;
we keep the fire, we keep the door,
we keep each other, and we keep still.

[po:verse,!condolences,warmly] Between your fire and mine
are hills and weather and a winding line
of road, and every letter goes
the long way round, the way the river flows.
But it arrives. That is the thing.
It always does. And so I sing.

[po:verse,!condolences] I planted a {PLANT} by the door
to see if it would grow;
it did, and now it blocks the door,
and I have to go round, and slow.

[po:verse,!condolences] A letter is a little house
you carry in your hand,
with someone sitting by the fire
in it, from another land.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:spacer] The light from that star left before I was born,
it crossed the long dark without stopping to rest;
it will never arrive at the far end of the sky,
it arrives only here, at my window, a guest.

So when you look up from your side of the hills
and you find the same star, with your letter begun,
remember it's old, and it travelled for you,
and it shines on us both, and it does not mind sharing the one.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:industrial|w:spacer] The lamps hum low on the factory floor,
the clock hands crawl to four;
I've counted the bolts and I've counted the hours,
and I'm counting them still, and more.

But the shift will end and the sun will rise
on the roofs and the wires and the rain,
and I'll walk home with the light in my eyes,
and come back tonight again.

[po:verse,!condolences,empire,warm|cordial] At court the candles never fail,
the floors are glass, the walls are gold;
the music never quite begins,
the soup is never hot, nor ever cold.

I would not change it for the world.
I tell myself so every night.
And then I read your letter, friend,
and wonder if I have it right.

[po:verse,!condolences,ours] At {COLONY} the evenings are long,
and somebody always has a song,
and somebody always has a complaint,
and somebody's always out of paint.

But the roof holds up and the fire holds in,
and we're all of us here, and that's a win;
so here's a verse from our side of the hill,
from all of us here, who are here still.

[po:lament,grave] We laid them down where the {TREE} stands
and the ground is soft in the rain;
we gave them back to the patient land
that gives us all again.

We will not say that they are sleeping,
for they would laugh at that;
we will say they did their share of the work
and left us where they sat.

And when the wind comes over the hill
and the long grass bends and sighs,
we will set a place at the table still,
and look away, and dry our eyes.

[po:lament,grave] There is a chair that no one takes,
a coat still on the peg,
a cup that someone always makes
and no one drinks. I beg

the days to hurry, and they don't;
the nights to pass, and they stay.
I say I'll mend, and think I won't,
and will, one day.

[po:lament,grave,warm|cordial] I cannot carry what you carry,
I cannot walk the road you walk;
but I can sit beside you, quietly,
and need no talk.

And when you are ready, I will listen,
and when you are not, I will wait;
the lamp is lit, the kettle's on,
and it is never late.

[po:lament,grave,!len:short] The bell rang once at morning,
the bell rang once at noon,
the bell rang once at evening
under a thin grey moon.

We counted all the ringing,
we counted all the lost,
we counted every candle
and every winter's frost.

And when the counting's over
and all the names are said,
we'll ring the bell for the living
as we rang it for the dead.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober] Fill up the cup and pass it along,
the night is short and the ale is strong;
the roof may leak and the fire may smoke,
but the cup goes round, and so does the joke.

Fill up the cup, it's a long way home,
the road is dark and the moon's gone to roam
off with the clouds like a dog with a bone;
so fill up the cup: you won't drink alone.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober] There's one barrel left and the winter is long,
so we'll drink it in measures and stretch it with song:
a sip for the harvest, a sip for the rain,
a sip for the neighbours who won't come again,
a sip for the goat, who has done nothing wrong,
and the rest for the singer who sings the last song.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober,!len:short] Oh, the brewer had a cellar and the cellar had a door,
and the door had a key, and the key was on the floor,
and the floor was in the dark, and the dark was full of rats,
and the rats were very drunk, and they were wearing little hats.

Oh, the brewer went down with a lantern in his hand,
and the rats struck up a waltz with a fiddle and a band,
and the brewer said, well, bother it, there's no use in being sour,
and he danced with them till morning, and was sober by the hour.

[po:hymn,c:pious] Before the dawn, before the bread,
before the work and the weather,
we give our thanks for those who wake
and those who sleep, together.

Keep watch on the road and the river and field,
keep watch on the ones we hold near;
and if there is grace left over to give,
we would not mind some here.

[po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] Praise to {DEITY} in the morning,
praise in the heat of the day,
praise when the lamps are lit at evening
and the children have finished their play.

Praise when the harvest is gathered,
praise when the harvest is thin;
the door of {DEITY}'s hall is open,
and all who are weary come in.

[po:hymn,c:nature] The tree does not ask to be thanked,
the river does not keep score;
the hill gives the hawk its wind for free,
and the sea asks nothing of the shore.

So we will take what we need, and no more,
and mend what we take with care,
and walk on the earth as a guest might walk
through a friend's home, gently, there.

[po:hymn,c:together,!condolences] One hand can lift a cup,
two hands can lift a beam,
a hundred hands can lift a roof,
a thousand lift a dream.

So give me your hand at the harvest,
and give me your hand in the snow,
and I'll give you mine when the road is long,
and wherever you go.

[po:work,c:herd,!condolences] Walk on, my slow ones, walk on easy,
the grass is sweet on the farther hill;
the sky is wide and the wind is breezy,
and the road is long, and there's time to kill.

Walk on, my slow ones, the river's waiting,
the evening's soft and the fire is near;
there's nobody chasing and nobody hating,
and nobody hurrying anyone here.

[po:work,!condolences,!w:tribal] Cut the corn and bind the sheaf,
the sun is hot and the day is brief;
one for the barn and one for the mill,
one for the birds on the windowsill,
and one for the one who works the least,
so they'll be quiet at the harvest feast.

[po:war,c:raider|c:martial,!condolences] Sharpen the blade on the long winter night,
mend the strap and the shield and the boot;
when the snow goes, the road will be ours by right,
and we'll come home heavy with loot.

Drink to the ones who will ride at our side,
and to those who rode out and did not come back;
the fire burns high and the hall is wide,
and we leave their cups where they hung, on the rack.

[po:nonsense,light] A goat went to market to buy a new hat,
and came back with a cabbage, a shovel, a cat;
the cat ate the cabbage, the shovel ran off,
and the goat wore the hat to a dance, with a cough.

[po:nonsense,light] There once was a cook at the edge of a town
who made a great pudding, three storeys and brown;
it stood in the square for a fortnight or more,
till {ANANIMAL} came by and went in at the door.

[po:nonsense,light] I asked the moon to dinner,
the moon said she was full;
I asked the sun to supper,
the sun said it was dull;
I asked the stars to breakfast,
they came, and stayed till noon,
and ate up all the porridge,
and never asked the moon.

[po:nonsense,light] My uncle kept a turnip that could whistle in the dark;
it whistled at the neighbours and it whistled at the lark,
it whistled at the weddings and it whistled at the dead,
until somebody boiled it, and we had soup instead.

[po:song,w:tribal] The fire is old. The fire is warm.
It was here before the hunt.
It will be here after the hunt.
Sit by it. Tell it your name.

The fire knows the names of the dead.
It says them in the smoke.
Watch the smoke go up.
Do not be afraid. It is only remembering.

[po:song,w:tribal,!condolences] Rain on the hide, rain on the stone,
rain on the old ones' bones;
the grass drinks, the {ANIMALS} drink,
the river grows, and the people sing.

[po:song,w:tribal] Feet, carry me.
Sky, cover me.
Path, know me.
Fire at the end of it, wait for me.

[olde,po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] Come list, and I will tell thee true
how once the waters rose,
and how the miller's daughter stood
where yet the alder grows.

She called the town unto the mill,
the young, the old, the lame,
and they did sit upon the sacks
and sing to keep from shame.

And when the grey morn came at last
the river heard the song,
and bowed its back and went its way,
for it had stayed too long.

[olde,po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] A knight rode out from the castle gate
with a lance and a borrowed horse,
to win the hand of a lady fair
and a purse of gold, of course.

He fought a bear, he fought a bull,
he fought a man in black,
and every time he won the fight
he lost the purse, and came back.

And now he keepeth a little farm
with a goat and a borrowed plough,
and the lady fair is wed to the bull,
and the knight is happier now.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences,season:winter] The snow lieth deep upon the wold,
the hearth is warm, the night is cold;
Heaven keep thee, friend, where'er thou art,
and keep a corner of thy heart
for us, who sit and think of thee
when the long dark lieth on the lea.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences,season:spring] Now cometh spring with mud and rain,
the lambs are loud, the plough is out;
I think of thee, and think again,
and wonder what thou art about.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences] A letter is a little hall
that one may carry in the hand,
with someone seated by the fire
within it, from another land.

[olde,po:lament,grave] They laid our friend beneath the yew
where the cold rain falleth slow,
and all the folk our friend e'er knew
stood weeping in a row.

Weep not, our friend would say to us,
for rest is come at last;
but set a cup out, even thus,
and drink, when grief is past.

[olde,po:lament,grave,warm|cordial] I may not bear the load thou bearest,
nor walk the road that thou must go;
but I will sit with thee, if thou carest,
and keep the watch till the fire is low.

[olde,po:drinking,light,!p:sober] Bring forth the cup and fill it high,
and let the sorry world go by;
the roof may leak, the rain may fall,
but here is ale enough for all.

Bring forth the cup and fill it full,
the night is long, the day was dull;
and if thou drink'st thy fill and more,
we'll bear thee home, as oft before.

[olde,po:hymn,c:pious] At dawn we praise, at noon we pray,
at eventide we bless
the bread, the roof, the one more day,
and all our neighbours' rest.

[olde,po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] Praise be to {DEITY} at break of day,
and praise when the sun is high,
and praise when the lamps are lit at eve
and the stars come out in the sky.

[olde,po:nonsense,light] A knight rode forth upon a goose,
his armour made of cheese;
he challenged every man he met,
and fell at every breeze.

[olde,po:work,!condolences] Reap the field and bind the sheaf,
the sun is hot, the day is brief;
one for the lord and one for the mill,
one for the birds upon the sill,
and one for him that laboureth least,
that he be quiet at the feast.

[sv:fey,po:song] By root and ring, by dew and stone,
this song is yours, and yours alone;
sing it once at the edge of night,
and the ring will know you, and treat you right.
By stone and dew, by ring and root,
we close the song, and the song is mute.

[sv:fey,po:song,!condolences] Three hops to the left of the old oak's shadow,
two to the right of the moon on the meadow,
there is a door that is not a door,
and we will be there, as we were before.

[sv:green,po:song] Slow light,
slow root,
the rain comes down
and we drink it, and we are glad.
The sun comes back
and we turn to it,
all of us, together, without hurry.

[sv:green,po:song] A seed is a letter
written to the spring.
We are writing to you
the same way.

[sv:machine,po:verse,!condolences] VERSE 1 OF 1.
THE SUN ROSE AT 0613.
IT WAS ADEQUATE.
I OBSERVED IT FOR FOURTEEN MINUTES,
WHICH WAS NOT REQUIRED.

[sv:machine,po:verse,light] ATTEMPT 7 AT RHYME:
THE RAIN FALLS ON THE ROOF.
THE ROOF IS WATERPROOF.
THIS IS BOTH A FACT AND PROOF.
I AM TOLD THIS SOUNDS ALOOF.

[sv:ancient,po:song] In the old tongue this was sung at the turning of the year, and took a night to sing. I give you the last verse only, which is the part everyone remembered.

Let the cold come; it has come before.
Let the dark come; it has gone before.
We are still at the table.
Pour.
